tour.title: Ipanema & Copacabana: Beaches, Lagoa & Arpoador
tour.summary: A flat beach-and-lagoon walk across the South Zone — Ipanema's sand, the Arpoador headland, Copacabana's wave-patterned promenade, a 1923 palace, and the lagoon behind it all.
tour.overviewText:
Rio's famous looks are geology you can read from the sand. The granite monoliths — Sugarloaf at the mouth of the bay, Corcovado behind the city, the Two Brothers over Leblon — are worn stumps of ancient mountains; between them the sea has drowned old valleys, leaving lagoons like Rodrigo de Freitas and the long beaches of Ipanema and Copacabana. Flat land is scarce here, so the city is long and thin, pressed between water and rock. That squeeze explains a lot: why the wealthy live on the sand, why the poor live on the hillsides above them, and why the beach is less a place Cariocas visit than a thing they are.

Cariocas — the word for a resident of this city, from a Tupi phrase meaning roughly "the white man's house" — run their year by the sea. The praia, the beach, is where Rio plays football and footvolley, argues politics, worships and mourns. On New Year's Eve millions wear white and jump seven waves as an offering to Iemanjá, the Yoruba goddess of the sea, a ritual carried over from Candomblé, the Afro-Brazilian religion that survived slavery and still shares the city with its Catholic majority. It is also where the city's defining inequality is plainest: look up from the sand and you see favelas — informal, self-built hillside neighbourhoods, home to more than a million Cariocas — stacked above some of the most expensive property in South America. Rio was Brazil's capital until Brasília took the job in 1960, hosted the World Cup in 2014 and the Olympics in 2016, and is still arguing about what those billions actually bought.

This walk stays on the flat. It starts in the middle of Ipanema, follows the sand to the Arpoador headland, turns into Copacabana and its wave-patterned promenade, passes the palace that made the neighbourhood fashionable, then rides the metro back to the canal and lagoon behind Ipanema and finishes at the water's edge, with Christ the Redeemer on the hill above.

Practically: about 11 km if you walk every metre, but the Copacabana-to-Ipanema stretch is 4.8 km of traffic-heavy streets, so ride the metro instead and the walking drops to about 7 km. It is flat throughout. You are here in the southern winter, mild and mostly dry, roughly 18–30°C, and the sun sets a little after 5pm, so start early afternoon. Carry water, small notes and a card; the currency is the real (R$). Watch your phone on the sand and after dark; swim only between the flags, and never just after heavy rain, when the sea carries the city's sewage. Christ the Redeemer and Sugarloaf are separate trips, not stops here: Corcovado by train or van, Sugarloaf by cable car.

Everything on this route is free to walk; only food, drink and transport cost money. Start at Posto 9.
tour.difficulty: Easy. Flat the whole way, on pavement or firm sand; the only climb is the steps up Arpoador rock, which you can skip. The middle leg is a metro ride, not a walk — on foot it would be a long, hot slog along heavy traffic.
tour.bestTimeOfDay: Start early afternoon, around 1 to 2pm. In the southern winter (June–July) the sun sets a little after 5pm, so that timing gives you room for the stops and puts you at Arpoador or the lagoon for the last light. Mornings are quieter and cooler. On Sundays one lane of Avenida Atlântica closes to cars and the promenade becomes a bike track.

stops.name: Ipanema Beach — Posto 9
stops.narration:
Welcome to Ipanema, and specifically to Posto 9. A posto is a lifeguard tower, and because Rio's beaches are enormous, each stretch is known by its number — and each number has a personality. Posto 9, in front of Rua Joana Angélica, is the bohemian one: students, artists, old radicals. Posto 8 is the LGBTQ+ stretch; Posto 10, families; Posto 7, toward Arpoador, the surfers. Choosing a posto is choosing a tribe.

Posto 9 got its reputation in 1979, when Fernando Gabeira — a former urban guerrilla from the MR8 group, which had kidnapped the American ambassador in 1969 — came home from exile and was photographed here in a skimpy purple swimsuit. The photograph scandalised and delighted the country and fixed Posto 9 as the counterculture address; he later became a congressman.

Now the name. Ipanema is Tupi, the language of Brazil's coastal indigenous peoples, and means, roughly, "stinking water" or "worthless water" — ipá, pond, plus nem-a, stinking. The name belonged to a river in São Paulo; it was pinned on this neighbourhood by a 19th-century nobleman, the Baron of Ipanema, who began settling the land in the 1880s. So the most glamorous beach in the world is named after bad water, and the district named after a man from somewhere else. Rio is like this: the myth is thin, the story underneath is better.

Stand facing the sea and you are looking at the open Atlantic, not a sheltered bay. Turn around: the hills rising behind the buildings are the Cantagalo and Pavão-Pavãozinho favelas, directly above some of the most expensive apartments in the country. That vertical gap of a few hundred metres is the shortest way to see Rio's inequality — same view, different world.

Ipanema also gave the world bossa nova. In the late 1950s, in bars just behind you, young musicians slowed samba down, stripped it to a nylon-string guitar and a whispered voice, and called it bossa nova — bossa being old slang for a knack, a way of doing something with flair. The song that reached the world was "The Girl from Ipanema", written in 1962: melody by Antônio Carlos Jobim, Portuguese lyrics by Vinícius de Moraes, English lyrics later by Norman Gimbel. Jobim composed it at his house on Rua Barão da Torre, a few streets inland, inspired by a real teenager, Helô Pinheiro, who walked past the Bar Veloso on her way to the sea. The bar is still there, renamed Bar Garota de Ipanema. The worldwide hit was the 1964 recording by Stan Getz and João Gilberto, with Astrud Gilberto's English vocal; it won the Grammy for Record of the Year and is said to be the second-most-recorded pop song in history. A neighbourhood named after stinking water exported a song about a girl walking to the beach.

Before you leave, look at what people are doing on the sand. Footvolley — volleyball played with the feet, head and chest, hands forbidden — was invented in Brazil in the 1960s and is played here constantly, along with beach football. Beach vendors sell mate (iced tea with lemon), coconut water and biscuits; the praia is a workplace as much as a playground, and a polite "não, obrigado" is enough.

Two practical things. First, the sea: swim between the flags near a lifeguard post — the Atlantic rips here are strong and people drown every year, usually visitors — and after heavy rain skip the water entirely, because Rio's storm drains overflow into the sea. Second, the sand: keep phones and cash out of sight, don't leave bags while you swim, and don't walk the beach after dark. That is not drama, just the arithmetic of a crowded public place.

When you're ready, turn left along the sand, with the Two Brothers behind you on your right, and walk about 1.5 km to the granite headland ahead. That is Arpoador.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free. The beach is public. Vendors sell food, drinks and chairs at their own prices — agree the price before you accept anything.
stops.openingHours: Open at all times. Lifeguards (the fire brigade) are generally on duty during daylight; the beach is busiest from late morning to sunset.
stops.accessibility: The sand is soft and hard to cross in a wheelchair; the promenade behind you is flat and paved. Ask a lifeguard about beach wheelchairs, which are sometimes available.
stops.insiderTip: Two blocks inland on Rua Vinícius de Moraes is the bar where Jobim and Vinícius de Moraes watched Helô Pinheiro walk to the sea; it is now called Bar Garota de Ipanema. Order a beer and look at the photographs on the wall.
stops.nextStopDirections: Turn left along the sand — the Two Brothers will be behind you on your right — and walk about 1.5 km to the granite headland at the end of the beach. That is Arpoador.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Mariordo (Mario Roberto Duran Ortiz), CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Arpoador Rock
stops.narration:
You are standing on Arpoador, the granite headland between Ipanema and Copacabana. The name comes from arpoar, to harpoon: in the colonial period fishermen used this rock as a lookout, waiting for whales to come close enough to hunt. Rio's most romantic sunset spot is named for whaling.

Look west and you have the postcard: Ipanema beach running away to Leblon, with the twin granite peaks of the Two Brothers at the far end. Look east and Copacabana curves north toward Sugarloaf, the 396-metre sugar-loaf-shaped monolith that marks the entrance to Guanabara Bay — the bay the city was founded on in 1565. Behind you, inland, Corcovado rises with Christ the Redeemer on top. Sugarloaf, Corcovado and the Two Brothers are all made of the same ancient granite and gneiss, hundreds of millions of years old, which erosion has worn down to stumps while the softer rock around them washed away. The same geology made the beaches: sand is just ground-up mountain, delivered here by rivers and the sea.

Below you, between this rock and Copacabana, is the Praia do Arpoador — barely 500 metres long and known as the surfers' beach. The rock creates a stable left-hand wave that can run three metres high in winter, one of the best metropolitan surf breaks in the world, and the crowd in the water is ferocious because the take-off zone is tiny and a rip current along the point drags you back out fast. If you don't surf, stay out of that patch; the rip is a conveyor belt for people who know it and a trap for people who don't.

Now the honest part about the sunset. Everyone calls Arpoador the sunset place, and it is — but the famous version, the sun dropping straight into the ocean, only happens around midsummer, in December and January. That is rare on a coast that mostly faces east: only then does the sun set far enough south to land in the water here. You are here in the southern winter, when the sun sets to the north-west — over the city, the lagoon and the hills, not the sea. It is still the best seat in Rio for the last hour of light, and Cariocas applaud when it goes down, a genuinely local habit. Just know what you are watching: the sun setting over the city you have been walking through.

The rock itself is open to the public, with steps and walkways cut into it; it is steep and uneven, and can be slippery after rain, so wear shoes with grip and don't crowd the edge. It is not step-free — the promenade at the base is flat, but the viewpoint is up steps. And because this is a famous sunset spot, it draws pickpockets at the same hour it draws crowds; keep your phone in a pocket, not a hand.

The small beach just east of here, tucked under the fort, is the Praia do Diabo — Devil's Beach — and beyond it the wall of Fort Copacabana, built in 1914, which in July 1922 was the scene of the Revolta dos 18 do Forte, a doomed army mutiny that became a founding legend of Brazilian reformism. In 2016 the fort's waters hosted the Olympic marathon swimming, and Copacabana beach next door hosted beach volleyball. Rio likes to stage its spectacles on the sand, and it was doing so long before the Olympics.

Walk down the Copacabana side of the rock to the beach and turn right along the promenade. Our next stop is about 2.2 km along the waterfront.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free. The rock and the promenade around it are public. No ticket, no gate.
stops.openingHours: Open at all times. Best in the hour before sunset, when the viewpoint gets crowded. Steps can be slippery after rain.
stops.accessibility: Not step-free: the viewpoint is reached by steps and uneven rock. The promenade at the base is flat and paved.
stops.insiderTip: Come about forty minutes before sunset; Cariocas applaud when the sun disappears, so join in. And note the winter geometry — right now the sun sets over the city, not the sea. The over-the-ocean version is a summer show.
stops.nextStopDirections: Walk down the Copacabana side of the rock to the beach and turn right along the promenade. Follow the waterfront about 2.2 km to the next stop on Copacabana beach.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Jenna Post, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Copacabana Beach & Promenade
stops.narration:
You are on Copacabana beach, and under your feet is one of the most famous pavements on earth. The calçadão — the Portuguese word for a wide paved seaside promenade — is set with pedra portuguesa, "Portuguese stone": thousands of small black and white cobbles laid by hand, a craft brought from Portugal in the 19th century. The wave pattern was laid when the promenade was rebuilt in 1970 by Roberto Burle Marx, Brazil's greatest landscape architect. His trick was scale: the mosaic is not meant to be read from your feet, where it looks like noise, but from above — the hotel balconies — where it resolves into an abstract painting that shifts as you move. He liked public work for a stated reason: public spaces, he said, give dignity to the masses.

Now the name. Copacabana was originally Sacopenapã, Tupi for something like "the way of the herons". It was renamed in the 18th century after a chapel here was given a copy of a statue of the Virgin of Copacabana, the patron saint of Bolivia. So this beach, the most famous in Brazil, is named for a Bolivian Madonna.

For most of the 19th century Copacabana was a remote strip of sand beyond the mountains. What changed it was engineering: a tunnel cut through the hills from Botafogo in 1892, Avenida Atlântica extended along the beach in 1919, and in 1923 the Copacabana Palace. Suddenly the beach was reachable and fashionable, and Copacabana became the Princesinha do Mar, the Little Princess of the Sea. The four-kilometre beach you are looking at, from Posto 1 at Leme to Posto 6 under the fort, is the result.

It is also a neighbourhood: about 160,000 people live here, one of the densest districts in the city and one of the oldest — roughly a quarter of residents are over 60. That is why you see the particular Copacabana scene: old men in tiny swimsuits playing cards at the kiosks. Next door, Ipanema was laid out later as a planned grid — quieter, richer, more residential, and by the 1960s the bohemian address. Copacabana is bigger, older and more democratic: grand hotels and cheap guesthouses, tourists and retirees, mixed on one beach.

Look along the sand and you are watching a social contract in action. The beach is divided by unspoken rules: football and footvolley near the postos, families in one stretch, the posing and the fit in another, fishing at dawn. Nobody enforces it; everyone knows it. And on New Year's Eve more than two million people in white pack this sand for one of the world's largest fireworks shows, jumping seven waves at midnight for Iemanjá — a tradition that began with Candomblé and Umbanda gatherings in the 1950s.

Two big-money events also landed here. The 2014 World Cup cost Brazil around US$11.6 billion, the most expensive ever at the time, and provoked mass protests — "Não vai ter Copa", there will be no Cup — over stadium spending while hospitals and transport went short. The 2016 Olympics cost about US$4.6 billion and left the city a real gift and a real hangover: a new metro line, Line 4, opened weeks before the Games — the line you will ride shortly — while promises to clean Guanabara Bay and the lagoon were dropped, and several venues were left unused. Supporters call the Games a coming-out for South America's first Olympic city; critics point at the bills that followed.

Safety, plainly: this is the ocean, not a pool. Swim between the flags, near a lifeguard post; red means stay out. Never swim after heavy rain — the storm drains flush sewage into the sea. Keep phones and valuables out of sight on the sand; the risk is opportunistic theft, not violence, and don't walk the beach after dark.

Our next stop is the white palace along the promenade.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free. Kiosks, beach chairs and umbrellas charge their own prices; the promenade and the sand are public.
stops.openingHours: Open at all times. Liveliest from late afternoon into the night; Sunday, when one lane of Avenida Atlântica closes to cars, is the busiest day.
stops.accessibility: Flat, wide, step-free promenade along the whole beach — the easiest walking on this route.
stops.insiderTip: Look at the wave mosaic from a higher floor if you can — a hotel bar or a friend's window. From the pavement it is just stones; from above it is a painting.
stops.nextStopDirections: Continue along the promenade about 1.2 km to the white palace with the columns — Copacabana Palace, at Avenida Atlântica 1702.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Donatas Dabravolskas, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Copacabana Palace
stops.narration:
This white building with the grand columns is the Copacabana Palace, and it is the reason Copacabana became famous. It opened on 13 August 1923, designed by the French architect Joseph Gire, who modelled it on two hotels of the French Riviera — the Negresco in Nice and the Carlton in Cannes. It was built by the Guinle family at the urging of Brazil's president, Epitácio Pessoa, who wanted a grand hotel to receive the visitors of the 1922 Independence Centenary Exposition; the government sweetened the deal with tax breaks and a casino licence. The Carrara marble and Bohemian crystal had to be imported, the foundations went fourteen metres down, and in 1922 a violent undertow destroyed Avenida Atlântica and flooded the hotel's lower floors before it had even opened. Mistinguett, the most famous French cabaret star of the day, came for the opening — and was forbidden from showing her celebrated legs.

For the next decades this was the address in South America. The casino made it a magnet for money and scandal, and the guest list reads like a century of celebrity: Walt Disney, Marlene Dietrich, Orson Welles, Josephine Baker, Brigitte Bardot, later Mick Jagger, Madonna, Princess Diana, Freddie Mercury, Lady Gaga. There is even a shooting: in 1928 President Washington Luís was shot here by his mistress and was officially reported to be suffering from appendicitis. Rio has always preferred a good story to a tidy one.

The hotel's luck turned with the country's. In 1946 Brazil banned gambling, and the casino became a concert hall — the Golden Room, opened in 1938 with a performance by Maurice Chevalier, is still there. In 1960 the capital moved to Brasília and Rio lost the political class that had filled the suites; through the 1970s the hotel slid. By 1985 it was slated for demolition, and was saved only when it was listed as a cultural property at federal, state and municipal level. In 1989 it was sold and lavishly restored, became a Belmond hotel in 2014, and in 2018 Belmond was bought by the French luxury group LVMH. The old lady survives by becoming expensive again.

Here is the practical bit, and it matters: the Copacabana Palace is not a museum. It is a working five-star hotel, and you cannot simply walk in and tour it — the lobby and restaurants are for guests and diners. The public beach in front is free and open to everyone, as Brazilian beaches are; the sand belongs to no one, which is a principle worth remembering in a city this unequal. If you want to see inside, the way in is to book afternoon tea or a drink at the bar, at hotel prices; check the dress code, book ahead, and verify times and prices at the desk or online.

Photographers: the classic shot is from the promenade, framing the white facade with the black-and-white wave mosaic running across the foreground — the two symbols of Copacabana in one frame. Late afternoon, when the building goes gold, is the best light.

From here our route turns inland. Walk about 550 metres up to Cardeal Arcoverde metro station and ride Line 1/4 four stops to Jardim de Alah. On foot it is 4.8 km along heavy traffic — about an hour — so don't. A single fare is a few reais; buy a card or tap at the gate, and check the current fare, since it changes. The metro is safe, fast and air-conditioned, and — as you'll hear — it is itself an Olympic leftover.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free to see from the promenade, but the hotel itself is not a tourist attraction you can tour. The only way inside is as a guest or a paying diner — book afternoon tea or a drink, at hotel prices. Verify at the desk.
stops.openingHours: The hotel operates around the clock, but it is not open to casual visitors. Its restaurants and bar keep their own hours; check and book ahead.
stops.accessibility: The promenade outside is flat and step-free. The hotel entrance has steps; if you have a booking, ask the staff about the accessible route.
stops.insiderTip: The classic photograph is from the promenade: the white facade behind the black-and-white wave mosaic. Go in the last hour of daylight, when the building turns gold.
stops.nextStopDirections: Walk about 550 metres inland to Cardeal Arcoverde metro station and ride Line 1/4 four stops to Jardim de Alah — a few minutes. On foot the same trip is 4.8 km of busy streets, about an hour, so don't. Check the current fare at the gate.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: MBIHund, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Jardim de Alah Canal
stops.narration:
You have come back through the hills on Line 4 and stepped out at Jardim de Alah, the canal that separates Ipanema from Leblon. This is the hinge of the whole landscape, so let's read it properly.

The water in front of you is a canal, and it exists for a reason that has nothing to do with beauty. Lagoa Rodrigo de Freitas, the lagoon up ahead, is a coastal lagoon — a body of water cut off from the ocean by a sandbar. It collects rain and stream water from the hills, and for centuries it stagnated, bred mosquitoes and smelled; a lagoon with no outlet is a lagoon that poisons itself. So in the early 1920s the city dredged this channel to reconnect the lagoon to the sea, letting the tide flush it twice a day. A carved stone dated 1922 marks the work, and the soil dug out of the channel was piled up to make one of the lagoon's islands. The whole thing is sanitation engineering disguised as a garden.

The garden came in 1938: a French-style park of pergolas, benches, almond trees and flowering sibipiruna, laid along both banks. It was named Jardim de Alah after the 1936 Hollywood film "The Garden of Allah", starring Marlene Dietrich and Charles Boyer. So a park in Rio is named after an American movie about a desert — a reminder that this city has been shaped by imported fantasies as much as by its own geology.

Now look north, up the canal, and think about what flows down it. The lagoon's water quality is a running battle. Streams coming off the hills, including a channelled river called Rio dos Macacos, carry untreated sewage; the exchange with the sea helps, but it never quite wins. When the lagoon hosted the Olympic rowing in 2016, athletes and doctors openly worried about infection, and they had cause: a year earlier, thirteen American rowers fell ill after a test event here. The city had promised to clean the lagoon and the bay for the Games; the promise outlasted the Games only slightly. If you see a rowing shell or a paddleboard out there, know that the water is better than it was and still not clean.

There is a harder story in this ground. The hills around the lagoon — Catacumba, and a favela called Praia do Pinto — once housed more than fifty thousand people in self-built houses. In 1969 a fire destroyed Praia do Pinto; the following year the authorities removed the residents, demolished the hills and used the rubble as landfill, moving the people out to the distant suburbs. The middle-class neighbourhood you are standing in was built on that erasure. Rio's beauty and Rio's inequality are not two stories; they are the same story told from different sides of the canal.

Practically: the canal water is not for swimming, ever. The park and the canal-side paths are level and easy, and the metro station makes this the most accessible point on the walk. Cross to the lagoon side and follow the water north about 1.5 km, keeping the lagoon on your left, to the kiosks at the water's edge. That is where we finish.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free park and canal-side walk. The metro fare to get here is separate.
stops.openingHours: Open at all times. The park is busiest in the morning and late afternoon; the metro station keeps metro hours.
stops.accessibility: Level paved paths along the canal and through the park; the metro station here has lifts.
stops.insiderTip: Find the carved stone dated 1922 at the beach end of the canal, marking the dredging that reconnected the lagoon to the sea. It is easy to miss behind the railings.
stops.nextStopDirections: Cross to the lagoon side and follow the canal and then the lagoon edge north about 1.5 km, keeping the water on your left, to the kiosks. That is the last stop.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Núcleo de digitalização / IMS, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Lagoa Rodrigo de Freitas
stops.narration:
This is Lagoa Rodrigo de Freitas — lagoa being the Portuguese word for lagoon — and it is the quiet centre of the Zona Sul, the South Zone. The lagoon covers about 2.4 million square metres, ringed by a paved path of 7.5 km that fills at dawn and dusk with runners, cyclists and rowers. The city ringed it with roads, too — Avenida Epitácio Pessoa and Avenida Borges de Medeiros — so the lagoon doubles as the great roundabout of the South Zone. Out on the water sit small islands: Piraquê, with the Naval Club; Caiçaras, with its waterski club. From here, if the light is right, you can see Christ the Redeemer on Corcovado above the trees.

The name is a marriage contract. In 1702 a Portuguese cavalry officer named Rodrigo de Freitas de Carvalho, eighteen years old, married Petronilha Fagundes, thirty-five, who had inherited this land. He went home to Portugal in 1717 and died there; she stayed. The lagoon has carried his name for three centuries, though before that it was called after her family. The people who lived here first, the Tamoio, called it Piraguá, "still water", or Sacopenapan, "path of the herons" — heron marshes, before they were a city.

Rio's history is not gentle, and this lagoon holds one of its cruellest chapters. In the 1570s the colonial governor, António Salema, wanted this land for a sugar mill. To clear it of the indigenous Tamoio without a war, he had clothing taken from people sick with smallpox laid along the banks, and waited. Smallpox did what he intended; the survivors were enslaved or driven off. The mill was built, and later, in 1808, when the Portuguese royal court fled Napoleon and moved to Brazil — the only European court ever to relocate to its own colony — the prince regent took the old mill site and founded a gunpowder factory and a royal botanical garden. That garden is now the Jardim Botânico, a short ride from here.

For all its calm, this is contested ground. The hills that once stood around the lagoon held those huge favelas, removed in 1970; the neighbourhood that replaced them, Lagoa, has one of the highest human development indices in Brazil. On the water, the rowing stadium hosted the 2016 Olympic rowing and canoe sprint, where the athletes' fear of the water quality was as much a story as the races. And every December a giant Christmas tree, built on a floating platform, is towed around the lagoon.

If you have energy left, the full circuit of the lagoon is 7.5 km, flat and paved and lit at night — one of the best urban walks in South America, and an easy way to see the whole social range of the South Zone in an hour. If you don't, do what Cariocas do: find a kiosk, order an água de coco — coconut water, drunk straight from the nut — and sit. The kiosks run late and take cards, but keep a few reais for the small vendors.

Two trips remain for another day. Christ the Redeemer, the 38-metre Art Deco statue finished in 1931, stands on the 710-metre Corcovado; the train up runs through Tijuca National Park, a forest replanted from the 1860s after coffee farms stripped the hills and threatened the city's water supply. Sugarloaf is reached by a cable car that has run since 1912. Neither is on this walk; both are visible from it, which is the point of Rio.

That is the end of the route. You have walked from Ipanema's sand to the lagoon behind it, and crossed the whole argument of this city: public beach and private wealth, mountain and water, the postcard and the people who make it work. Come back at sunset. The city is at its best then, and it knows it.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free to walk the lagoon edge and the 7.5 km circuit. Kiosks, boats and the rowing stadium charge separately.
stops.openingHours: Open at all times; the path is lit at night. Kiosks run late. The lagoon is busiest at dawn and dusk.
stops.accessibility: Flat, paved, step-free path around the whole lagoon — the most accessible stop on the walk.
stops.insiderTip: The full 7.5 km loop is the best hour you can spend in Rio if you still have legs. Otherwise, order coconut water at a kiosk and watch the rowers as the light goes.
stops.nextStopDirections: End of the walk. You can keep going around the lagoon on the 7.5 km circuit, sit at a kiosk, or walk back through Ipanema to the beach. Taxis are easy here, and the metro (Jardim de Alah, General Osório) is close if you would rather ride. Christ the Redeemer and Sugarloaf are separate trips for another day.
